sentences.text: Brighstoneus is a genus of hadrosauriform dinosaur belonging to the class Ornithischia, found in the Early Cretaceous Wessex Formation on the Isle of Wight, England.
The genus contains only one known species, Brighstoneus simmondsi, which is the type species of the genus.

The holotype — the specimen the species is based on — consists of a partial skeleton that includes the skull and lower jaws, featuring a unique nasal bulla where the nasal bone bulges upward past the nostril opening.

When viewed from the side, the dorsal surface of the nasal bone forms an almost entirely unique "S"-shape, and the maxillary process accounts for roughly 60% of the jugal bone's length, a proportion higher than in most hadrosauriforms.
The predentary bone features a bilobed, heart-shaped process on its underside, while the dorsal surface bears a series of large denticles.

The dentary row contains 28 tooth sockets, with a potential additional socket indicated by a small pit on the right dentary, holding the record for the highest number of alveoli among hadrosauriforms with active and replacement teeth in the same socket.
A 2024 estimate by Gregory S. Paul suggests Brighstoneus was approximately 6 meters long and weighed about 1 ton.
A high ridge ran along Brighstoneus' spine, with neural spines at the tail base exceeding 370% the height of the vertebral centra.

The holotype specimen MIWG 6344 was discovered in the summer of 1978 after a storm caused a collapse at Grange Chine, with the species name simmondsi honoring Keith Simmonds, who assisted in the discovery of the remains.

Remains initially thought to be Iguanodon generated significant interest in the early 1980s, leading to further collection efforts, before Brighstoneus was identified as distinct from Mantellisaurus in 2019 by Jeremy Lockwood during his PhD research at the University of Portsmouth.
Brighstoneus simmondsi was formally named and described in 2021 by Jeremy Lockwood, David Martill, and Susannah Maidment.
Only one fossil occurrence of Brighstoneus has been recorded.
The original description noted that Brighstoneus was large in size but did not provide specific estimates for dimensions or body mass.

Phylogenetic analyses in 2021 placed Brighstoneus within the clade Iguanodontia, and most analyses suggest it is a basal member of Hadrosauriformes, forming a polytomy with Barilium, Hypselospinus, Iguanodon, and Mantellisaurus.
One analysis excluding specific nasal and ilium characters recovered Brighstoneus outside Hadrosauriformes as a sister species to Ouranosaurus.

A 2024 study by Lockwood et al. recovered Brighstoneus as the earliest-diverging member of Hadrosauroidea within Hadrosauriformes, while a 2025 study by Bertozzo et al. recovered it as the sister taxon to a clade containing Comptonatus and Brighstoneus, placing these taxa within Hadrosauroidea after the Iguanodontidae.
A 2026 study by Huang et al. using an updated matrix recovered a comparable clade for these taxa.

The fossils date to the Barremian stage of the Early Cretaceous, approximately 125 million years ago, specifically between 125.77 and 121.4 million years ago, found in Barremian deposits of the Wessex Formation.
Brighstoneus lived on a floodplain environment intersected by rivers and lakes, where water levels varied seasonally due to high evaporation despite significant precipitation.
The environment experienced frequent extreme storms and floods that deposited dead organisms in ponds, and frequent wildfires occurred in the habitat, which prevented the dense growth of gymnosperms.
